newsitem.title: ARMENIA: Elections, crackdown dull Armenian leader's image.
newsitem.headline: Elections, crackdown dull Armenian leader's image.

text.p: Embattled Armenian President Levon Ter-Petrosyan still rules in his mountainous land, but his once-shining image has been tarnished by opposition charges that he has become an autocrat.

Ter-Petrosyan, 51, the last survivor among post-Soviet "poet kings", was officially declared the winner of last week's presidential election, but international observers say widespread fraud may have helped him steal the crown.
Official results gave him 51.8 percent of the vote, just enough to avoid a second-round showdown with former prime minister Vazgen Manukyan, who took 41.3 percent.
Manukyan's supporters reacted to the count with violent protests and Defence Minister Vazgen Sarkisyan said there was no chance that Manukyan could ever have taken power.
"Even if he got 100 percent of the vote, neither the army nor the interior ministry nor the security forces would accept him," he said.
Manukyan, a bespectacled 50-year old physicist, had promised to raise living standards quickly and said Ter-Petrosyan had lost touch with reality.
Most foreign observers say unofficially that, had the elections been fair, Ter-Petrosyan at best faced a runoff ballot and at worst outright defeat.
Diplomats say the aloof president used the protest by Manukyan supporters as a pretext to send the army into the streets, put dozens of detractors in prison and close political parties.
Manukyan has gone into hiding, fearing arrest.

Ter-Petrosyan's supporters complain the opposition took to the streets rather than seeking legal redress for their complaints about the count. The president, speaking on television on Monday night, said there would be no witchhunt.
He had earlier described the protests as a "fascist" coup by "mentally ill people".
Leading opposition figures who have not been arrested say the unrest was a convenient excuse for Ter-Petrosyan to wipe out dissent in this poverty-stricken country of 3.5 million.

Diplomats dismissed the idea that the protests, in which 59 people were hurt, were an attempt to topple the government. "I don't know if he (Ter-Petrosyan) actually believes this, but I can say that almost no one else does," said one, one who did not wish to be identified.
"This whole thing was nicely stage-managed and now Ter- Petrosyan doesn't have to deal with elections or an opposition," he said.

Diplomats and opposition sources say up to 250 people have been detained on political grounds and some have been beaten up, although the prosecutor's office says it knows nothing about large-scale arrests.
With parliament dominated by his ruling bloc Ter-Petrosyan runs a virtual one-party state.
The philologist president once belonged to a small group of anti-communist politicians including Georgia's Zviad Gamsakhurdia, Lithuania's Vitautas Landsbergis and Azerbaijan's Albufaz Elchibey.
All were academics or cultural figures who played big roles in leading their republics to independence from the former Soviet Union.
Now Gamsakhurdia is dead, Landsbergis has left office and Elchibey lives in exile. Ter-Petrosyan, once a darling of the west, has seen his image as a democrat all but obliterated.
"If there were any doubts before that he is not a democrat, then this has erased them all," said the diplomat.
But the envoy expected few repercussions.
"Very few people in this country have any real idea of what democracy means. I doubt things would have been much different regardless of who was in power."
